introduction.text: The Basilica di Sant'Andrea delle Fratte is a 17th‑century Roman Catholic basilica in Rome, dedicated to St. Andrew. It is notable for its Baroque architecture, its rich interior art, and its historical role as the national church of the Scots in Rome and later as a minor basilica.

history.description: The original church on the site was erected in 1192.
In 1585 Pope Sixtus V assigned the church to the Minim friars of Saint Francis of Paola.
Construction of the new church began in 1604 under the design of Gaspare Guerra.
In 1653 the project was revamped by Francesco Borromini, who designed the apse, the tholobate of the cupola, and the square campanile.
The late Renaissance façade, completed in 1826, was funded by the Testament of Cardinal Ercole Consalvi.
In 1942 Pope Pius XII elevated the church to the rank of a minor basilica.

design.description: The basilica features a single nave with three chapels on each side and a square campanile with four orders.
The façade is a late Renaissance style with two orders divided by pilasters.
The square campanile, designed by Borromini, is a prominent Baroque feature.

art.description: The cupola is decorated by Pasquale Marini.
A wooden tempietto painted by Borgognone (Jacques Courtois) dates to 1674.
The Baptism of Christ in the first chapel is by Ludovico Gimignani.
The funeral monument of Cardinal Pierluigi Carafa was sculpted by Pietro Bracci.
Frescoes in the cloister depict the Life of Saint Francesco by Marini, Cozza, and Gherardi.
Two angels by Bernini, originally intended for Ponte Sant'Angelo, are displayed at the presbytery.
